title: After 30 years they finally let Ace Combat's director fly in a real jet, and I'm taking credit
summary: This is what a man looks like after fulfilling a lifelong dream.
body: Kazutoki Kono: You're welcome. Back in June , I asked the Ace Combat brand director, who's been working on the series since 1997's Ace Combat 2, if he'd ever gotten to strap into an F-16 and experience the real thrills of doing barrel rolls at 30,000 feet. "Unfortunately over the last 30 years of my career I've been appealing, saying 'hey, we want to ride in one of these jets!' but we have not yet had the chance," Kono said at the time. "Neither myself, or anyone on the team." Mere months later, it's a whole new world. In a promotional video released today alongside Ace Combat 8, Bandai Namco revealed that Kono finally got to climb into the cockpit of a jet and live the real life version of the series he's been overseeing for years and years. Well, minus the combat parts. "I was scared before getting in. But once we were airborne, it turned into one of the most beautiful experiences," he said in the video. "The G-force during turns was noticeable, but what stood out the most was the force pushing me downward into the seat. Being up in the sky inside such a compact cockpit felt incredible. It was a surprisingly comfortable and enjoyable space to be in. Compared to a large aircraft,…

title: Dear former NFL head coach Mike Tomlin: Your 12-year Minecraft city is beautiful
summary: It may or may not have contributed to the Steelers' years of postseason woes—but at least it's walkable.
body: By the time he stepped down as head coach of the Pittsburgh Steelers in 2025, Mike Tomlin—then the NFL's longest-tenured coach—had led the team through a 19-year run without a losing season, securing 13 playoff appearances, eight division titles, and a victory at Super Bowl XLIII. Since 2014, however, Tomlin has been answering a higher calling: He's been building. In a YouTube video on Wednesday, he unveiled his true masterwork: A sprawling Minecraft metropolis that he's been meticulously hand-sculpting for the last 12 years. And it's magnificent. As the video starts, Tomlin—PlayStation controller in hand—explains that he was introduced to Minecraft by his children, who were obsessed with the game during their middle school years. While he didn't have much history with videogames, he was "mesmerized by what could occupy their attention," and as he's "always had an interest in architecture," he naturally gravitated to Minecraft's creative mode. Eventually, his kids moved on to other interests—but Tomlin remained transfixed by the "therapeutic" act of crafting buildings, communities, and neighborhoods. "It allowed me to detach from the realities and pressures of life," Tomlin says. …

title: The upcoming sim about making games is so deep your in-game game can even get cyberleeked
summary: Let's Build a Dungeon isn't just about making a game, but all the stuff you have to deal with while making a game.
body: Of all the games on the horizon, the one I may be most looking forward to Let's Build a Dungeon . It's a sim from Springloaded, makers of Let's Build a Zoo and the upcoming RollerCoaster Tycoon Wonderworks , and the premise is one we've all mulled at one point or another: what if I could make my own videogame? And in Let's Build a Dungeon, you can. Dig dungeons, populate them with monsters and traps and loot, design quests, and watch simulated players play your game. You'll even be able to let real players play the game you make. But there's also the simulation surrounding the game you're building. The development studio you've founded. The devs you hire. You'll have to deal with investors, finances, the public, the press (like me!), crunch, gaming conventions, hackers, and even text messages from your mom. There's a lot going on in this sim. Like, a lot , a lot. During a recent preview and interview with Springloaded founder and Let's Build a Dungeon lead developer James Barnard , here's what leapt out at me as being the most a lot among the lot. "We have, like, 700 [fictional] games or something, and the list keeps on getting longer." James Barnard (Image credit: James Barnard) …

title: I'm going to teach you to love hidden object games
summary: Or at least to respect them. I'd settle for that. And if you feel like embarking on a journey of discovery, I can help with that, too.
body: It's a fact: Hidden object games have a less-than-stellar reputation among the gamer cognoscenti. They're commonly viewed as low effort, vacuous, beneath the notice or caring of real gamers⁠—a sort of proto-slop, in many ways, that predates the rise of AI. They're games your mom plays. Ewwww. Dramatic exaggeration? Not really. Back in 2016, we published a story entitled " My shameful obsession with hidden object games on Steam ," whose author chose to remain anonymous to avoid the consequences of their humiliating admission—and yeah, maybe that was a bit of dramatic exaggeration. But it vividly illustrates the point that hidden object games are not taken seriously by serious gamers. I'm here to change that. I'm here to tell you that hidden object games are good , actually, and that it's a valid genre worthy of respect. Because videogames can be anything. Yes, violence tends to be at the core of most mainstream gaming experiences, your Calls of Duty and your Dotas and your Grand Thefts Auto and whatnot. But there's so much more out there. You can drive a bus, manage a cycling team, collect mushrooms on another planet, or play weird card games. So what's the big deal about just sitt…

title: In my quest to find the perfect mouse for me, I've ended up with two completely different ones
summary: I guess I'm just picky.
body: The odd thing about computer mice—gaming, ergonomic, or otherwise—is how subjective they are. I guess we've all got different hand shapes, finger lengths, and technical needs. I've been hunting for the perfect mouse for my particular hands for years now, and I've refined my selection down to two. Unfortunately, they couldn't be more different, so I guess I'm a two-mouse sort of guy now. One is the Logitech MX Master 4 , an ergonomic mouse with a poor sensor for gaming, but an excellent shape for all-day work usage. It's also near-silent, which the rest of my household is very grateful for. (Image credit: Future) And the other is the Razer Cobra HyperSpeed , a tiny rodent with exactly the sort of weight and technical specs I like for gaming, all for a relatively reasonable sum. Looking at the two together, they're completely chalk and cheese. Neither mouse is perfect, but switching between the two is the best solution I've found for all my computing needs. As I sit here during a workday, typing out this article, it's the MX Master 4 that keeps me company. title: Metal desks nearly destroyed a Valorant tournament
summary: And players have been urged to switch to wired mice.
body: Wireless gaming mice are great and have only gotten better with time. They're so good, in fact, that I would not go for a wired model unless I was really looking for a budget option. And yet it turns out wired mice were the best choice for the Valorant Champions tournament in Shanghai, where custom desks were apparently interfering with the signal. The Valorant Esports X page recently revealed that "repeated mouse interference issues have caused multiple tech pauses and disrupted our most important tournament of the year" and that it would be asking all players to swap to wired mice until the problem is fixed. In a match between FUT Esports and 100 Thieves, player xeus had an issue with their mouse where it was unable to fire. Xeus is part of FUT, which lost to 100 Thieves, two to zero. Riot claims, "Following an official post-game evaluation, we concluded that a round rollback should have been allowed. We take responsibility for that error." title: Riot needed absurd player counts 'in the high hundreds of thousands, if not millions' for 2XKO, dooming it from launch
summary: The cost is too dang high.
body: 2XKO ending its development (which Merrill phrases here as turning it into a "box game" instead, despite the fact Riot also laid off a bunch of people to make that happen), came as a deep frustration, but not much of a surprise given the current nightmare year the industry's been having. However—that number, "high hundreds of thousands, if not millions", is a somewhat desperate number. Especially given the podcast has an annotation of monthly active users (MAU), which one'd assume would mean they asked Merrill for clarification. An active user is a unique user that logs in and does something at least once during a month, which means that the number would be far higher than concurrent users (how many of those users are logged in at any one time). However, we can at least make some very loose guesstimates. Street Fighter 6 has a 30,000 concurrent peak on PC at the time of writing. Let's assume the average person has a seven hour window during a day to play, accounting for a nine to five job or chores/social obligations on the weekend—the concurrent count doesn't actually jump that much. The Redditor bought the PC from a Micro Center in Tustin, California, and according to the manager, the new anti-export declaration only came into effect a few days ago. High-end GPUs have been banned from being exported to China as America is looking to win the AI race, and more beefy cards in the country equals more power. title: 'Open world fatigue' is one reason indie RPG Entropy is borrowing from the classics: 'PS1, PS2, GameCube games really never outstayed their welcome'
summary: Except Drakengard.
body: Indie RPG team Lovely Hellplace is undeniably retro-focused: 2024's Dread Delusion and the early access Entropy are crunchy and polygonal as hell. But that also extends to design. Dread Delusion was like a stripped-down Morrowind, while Entropy is a classico JRPG with some PC gaming DNA spliced in . When I spoke to lead developer James Wragg earlier this year, he told me that he thinks part of the appeal of older games is their willingness to be succinct. Elsewhere in our conversation, Wragg revealed that he's never beaten Breath of the Wild, and whenever he plays, he just wants to revisit 2002's Wind Waker instead. I find this issue much more acute on replays, in my own experience: I've never beaten BotW a second time after that initial playthrough where I got all the shrines (I was unemployed). More recently, I've found myself turning away from my beloved Elden Ring to the far more snackable Bloodborne and Sekiro. Fallout is such a good shout here: I had a fairly completionist replay a few years ago, and I wrapped it in about 12 hours. Even the fact that Wragg's previous game, Dread Delusion, was open world isn't as much of a gotcha as you might think: It's a pretty dense map an…

body: In the mere two days since The Witcher 3: Remastered released on PC, its Nexus Mods page has been a hive of activity, featuring updates for all sorts of customization packages for the game— including ones you'll only install if you're a coward . By my count, more than 450 Witcher 3 mods are either newly released or updated since September 29, an overwhelming number if you thought you'd just poke your head in and see what's been going on. One thing that's going on is that a lot of mods are now using AI image generation to create thumbnails that immediately give me the ick. Why create a fake, AI-glazed screenshot for your HUD mod when we all know what The Witcher 3 actually looks like? Baffling! Another thing that's going on, thankfully, is that some modders with names like GrimReaper2121 are still putting in good work with creations such as De-mastered Geralt . And loads of mods that date back to the 2010s, making them mainstays of The Witcher 3's mod scene, have been updated to play nice with the latest patch. Deep discounts up the wazoo, stickers to earn, and new stuff in the Points Shop , all of it adding up to Valve-powered seasonal trauma inflicted on your personal finances. And I know what you're thinking: Are there really more than 44,000 games for under $5 in the Autumn Sale? And the answer is "yes," according to SteamDB anyway: The "sales" option on the site lets you filter games by a range of options, including price—cap the list at five bucks and that's what comes out. (Image credit: SteamDB) In any event, it's a whole lotta deals, and the sheer volume of discounts on Steam means that some of these deeply-cheap games—maybe even a lot of 'em—probably aren't top-tier stuff. You might therefore want to apply more filters: You can set genre and feature tags, release dates, a minimum user rating or number of reviews, and all sorts of other things to winnow it out a bit. I like browsing as much as the next guy, but 2,105 games is a lot to dig through. title: You can now play Halo: Combat Evolved in a web browser, and it even has multiplayer
summary: Fancy a 1v1?
body: In an act that is both technically impressive and presumably legally dubious, a developer has got a build of the original Halo: Combat Evolved working in a web browser. And no, I didn't play the game instead of writing this article in a timely fashion; why do you ask? Developer Mitchell Hynes recently took to X to share their browser-based rendition of Halo , and it works surprisingly well. Simply click on the site, wait for the browser to download anything it needs, and start playing. It even has full mouse and keyboard support. It's all built off the decompilation project from Bnunu , who have been reverse-engineering the game for some time. It, combined with a fork from team Cybersecurity , supports 128-player multiplayer and works on Windows, Linux, and Android. The site saw so much traffic from X that it very briefly went down, as it was automatically flagged for "suspected phishing", but has since come back online. Within just five hours, the browser-based project saw almost 20,000 games across 115 countries, according to the developer . title: Don't fear the BIOS update: Asus has just fixed a local access vulnerability affecting older Intel motherboards
summary: To be clear, it's only older motherboards for 8th and 9th Gen Intel CPUs that are affected by the issue.
body: I'll be honest: BIOS updates give me the willies. Unfortunately, even as such a source of undue anxiety, they are still well worth staying on top of. Case in point, the latest BIOS update from Asus addresses a vulnerability found in motherboards for 8th and 9th Gen Intel chips. The vulnerability in question is described as "Improper initialization in an ASUS certain motherboard [sic] allows an physically proximate user to read or write arbitrary memory by inserting a specially crafted device." Basically, a bad actor would need to be in the same room as an affected PC to exploit this vulnerability. Even though local access is required, it's still a pretty serious issue. Designated CVE-2026-93495 , the issue has a high severity score of 7.0. As such, Asus has issued a security bulletin earlier today saying it "strongly recommends updating to the latest version" of the BIOS for a list of affected motherboards. The affected motherboards include a number of ROG Strix and ROG Maximus models. title: Google Japan's conveyor belt keyboard is a sad reminder of the sense of humour the whole company used to have long, long ago
summary: Google Japan has form, pity it's seemingly the only bit of Google that still does.
body: Is this a piss take? Okay, this is definitely a piss take. Google Japan has posted a YouTube video showcasing the new Gboard Conveyor Belt Version . What we are talking about here, people, is "a keyboard whose keys are delivered straight to your finger tips." Literally. Turns out, Google Japan has form with this kind of thing, what with the rotary keyboard and absurdly-long-stick-of-single-keys keyboard , er, keyboards they've done before. But this conveyor-belt board? This one might just be the best of all. The keyboard has four columns of vertically stacked keys that rotate on a belt, the idea being that you don't move your hand, you just wait for the right key to arrive. As the video explains, "just as conveyor belts ramped up factory productivity, we wondered if we could streamline typing in the exact same way." Well, quite. title: This arse cushion is the biggest upgrade I've made to my gaming setup in 2026, which says a lot about where we're at right now

body: Like many of you, I love upgrading my PC and anything to do with my gaming setup. So, I gave in and bought a cushion. It's magnificent, and has improved my comfort levels at least ten-fold in comparison to the firm seat of my steely-buttocked gaming chair.
